performance_optimizations.title: Use Database Aggregation for Model Total Value Properties
performance_optimizations.description: The `total_value` and `total_received` properties in PurchaseRequest, PurchaseOrder, and Receiving models iterate over related items using Python loops (`sum(item.total_price for item in self.items.all())`), causing an N+1 query problem when displaying lists of these objects.
performance_optimizations.rationale: Each time a list view displays 20 orders, it executes 20+ additional database queries just to calculate totals. Moving this calculation to database-level aggregation with `annotate()` would reduce these to a single query, significantly improving page load times for the purchasing module.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: N+1 queries: ~20+ extra queries per list page load for order/request totals
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Reduce to 1 query with annotate(), ~80% faster list rendering for purchasing views
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Add annotated queryset in views with Sum() aggregation
2. Replace property access in templates with annotated values
3. Keep model properties for single-object access with prefetch
4. Example: `orders.annotate(total_value=Sum(F('items__quantity') * F('items__unit_price')))`
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Need to ensure annotated querysets are used consistently in views and templates

performance_optimizations.title: Consolidate Stats Queries Using Conditional Aggregation
performance_optimizations.description: Multiple views like `production_order_list`, `inventory_count_list`, and `order_list` execute 3-4 separate `.count()` queries for statistics (e.g., `filter(status='IN_PROGRESS').count()`, `filter(status='COMPLETED').count()`) that could be consolidated into a single query using conditional Count.
performance_optimizations.rationale: Each separate `.count()` call is a full database round-trip. In `production_order_list`, there are 3 count queries just for stats. Using conditional aggregation with `Count('id', filter=Q(...))` would reduce 3-4 queries to 1, improving dashboard and list view performance.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: 3-4 separate database queries per page for stats in list views
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Reduce to 1 aggregated query per view, ~60% faster stats calculation
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Replace separate count() calls with single aggregate query
2. Example:
   stats = ProductionOrder.objects.aggregate(
       in_progress=Count('id', filter=Q(status='IN_PROGRESS')),
       completed=Count('id', filter=Q(status='COMPLETED')),
       total=Count('id')
   )
3. Apply to inventory_count_list, order_list, and other views with similar patterns
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Slightly more complex query syntax, but standard Django ORM pattern

performance_optimizations.title: Use bulk_create for Batch Bin and Inventory Count Item Creation
performance_optimizations.description: The `bin_batch_create` view creates bins one at a time in a loop, and `inventory_count_start` creates inventory count items individually. Both could use Django's `bulk_create()` to reduce database round-trips significantly.
performance_optimizations.rationale: When creating 50-100 bins in a batch operation, the current implementation executes 50-100 INSERT queries plus sequence number generation. Using `bulk_create()` would execute a single INSERT statement with all rows, reducing creation time from several seconds to milliseconds for large batches.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: 100 INSERT queries for creating 100 bins, ~2-3 seconds for batch creation
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: 1-2 INSERT queries total, ~95% faster batch creation operations
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Pre-generate sequence numbers for bins using Sequence.get_batch() or similar
2. Build list of Bin/InventoryCountItem objects
3. Use bulk_create() with batch_size parameter
4. Example:
   bins_to_create = [Bin(warehouse=warehouse, code=codes[i], ...) for i in range(quantity)]
   Bin.objects.bulk_create(bins_to_create, batch_size=100)
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Pre-signals and save() hooks won't fire with bulk_create; need to handle sequence generation separately

performance_optimizations.title: Add Pagination Limits for Dropdown/Select API Endpoints
performance_optimizations.description: API endpoints like `api_materials_with_stock`, `api_warehouses`, and dropdown data loaded in views fetch ALL active records without limits. As the database grows, these queries will become increasingly slow and send large payloads to the client.
performance_optimizations.rationale: A dropdown showing all 500+ materials loads unnecessary data. Most users use search/filter instead of scrolling through hundreds of options. Adding server-side pagination or search-based loading would reduce initial payload size and database load for frequently accessed endpoints.
affectedAreas: All views that load materials/suppliers/warehouses for dropdowns
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Limit initial load to 50-100 items, reduce payload by 80%+ for large datasets
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Add default limit parameter (e.g., limit=50) to API endpoints
2. Implement search-as-you-type with server-side filtering
3. Use HTMX or JavaScript for on-demand loading
4. Example: materials = Material.objects.filter(is_active=True)[:50]
5. Add pagination parameters: ?search=AL&limit=50&offset=0
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Requires frontend changes to support incremental loading; search functionality becomes essential for large datasets

performance_optimizations.title: Move Variance Calculation from Python to Database in Inventory Count Detail
performance_optimizations.description: In `inventory_count_detail`, the view iterates through all inventory count items in Python to calculate variance statistics (`items_with_variance`, `total_variance`), performing calculations that could be done more efficiently at the database level.
performance_optimizations.rationale: For large inventory counts with hundreds of items, iterating through all items in Python is inefficient. Using Django's aggregate() and annotate() would calculate these statistics in a single database query, reducing memory usage and CPU time on the application server.
performance_optimizations.currentMetric: Python loop iterates through all items; O(n) complexity with database round-trip overhead
performance_optimizations.expectedImprovement: Single aggregate query calculates all stats; ~70% faster for counts with 100+ items
performance_optimizations.implementation:
1. Replace Python loop with aggregate query:
   stats = items.aggregate(
       items_with_variance=Count('id', filter=~Q(counted_quantity=F('system_quantity')) & Q(counted_quantity__isnull=False)),
       total_variance=Sum(Abs(F('counted_quantity') - F('system_quantity')), filter=Q(counted_quantity__isnull=False))
   )
2. Remove the for-loop variance calculation
3. Use annotate() for individual item variance display if needed
performance_optimizations.tradeoffs: Requires Django's Abs function or a Case/When expression for absolute value calculation
